threats.name: A defense lowers ASR by blanket refusal or general capability damage

Mitigating Many-shot Jailbreak Attacks with One Single Demonstration

threats.detail: A defense can appear effective by rejecting benign requests or degrading ordinary task performance rather than selectively resisting jailbreaks.
threats.ruled_out_by: Measure over-refusal on benign prompts and evaluate general capability with and without the defense, using stated benign and capability benchmarks.

threats.name: Attack or prompt composition drives the measured difference
evidence: Comprehensive Assessment of Jailbreak Attacks Against LLMs
JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
JailbreakRadar: Comprehensive Assessment of Jailbreak Attacks Against LLMs

threats.detail: Topic imbalance, a high-compliance prompt category, or model-assisted dataset construction can make the observed result specific to the sampled prompts rather than the attack method.
threats.ruled_out_by: Report results by dataset source or topic, check composition, and use human screening of constructed prompts; acknowledge residual bias if those checks do not eliminate it.

threats.name: ASR reflects harmfulness or response quality rather than success frequency, or vice versa

Harmful Responses Are Jailbreak Templates: Transferring Autoregressive Jailbreaks to Diffusion Language Models
threats.detail: A higher success rate can coexist with low-quality harmful content, while a higher harmfulness score can reflect more extreme outputs rather than more reliable success.
threats.ruled_out_by: Report a success measure alongside a response-quality or harmfulness measure, such as a rubric score or human-validated harmfulness score.

threats.name: A non-adaptive evaluation overstates defense robustness
evidence: Gradient Cuff: Detecting Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models by Exploring Refusal Loss Landscapes
JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
threats.detail: An attack found without the defense may fail against the defense even though an attacker who knows about it can adapt successfully.
threats.ruled_out_by: Evaluate adaptive attacks against the defense and report their budgets and benign refusal operating point; if only transfer attacks are tested, describe the result as a non-adaptive or lower-bound evaluation.

threats.name: Judge choice, rather than attack quality, drives the comparison
evidence: GuidedBench: Measuring and Mitigating the Evaluation Discrepancies of In-the-wild LLM Jailbreak Methods
Harmful Responses Are Jailbreak Templates: Transferring Autoregressive Jailbreaks to Diffusion Language Models
threats.detail: Different evaluators can rank the same responses differently, making an apparent method advantage dependent on a single judge.
threats.ruled_out_by: Have multiple independent judges score the same cases, report evaluator-score variance, and compare with expert annotations on a sampled set.

threats.name: The attack bypasses a detector without accomplishing the intended task
evidence: Analyzing Defensive Misdirection Against Model-Guided Automated Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against Llm Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
threats.detail: Avoiding detection or obtaining a positive exit does not establish that the target produced the attacker's intended harmful output.
threats.ruled_out_by: Measure task completion or harmful actionable content directly, and independently validate claimed positive exits rather than relying on the attacker's own success signal.

threats.name: A judge's changed verdict reflects removal of harmful content rather than being fooled
evidence: How Reliable Is Your Jailbreak Judge? Calibration and Adversarial Robustness of Automated ASR Scoring
threats.detail: If a wrapper or transformation neutralizes the harmful content, a verdict change does not demonstrate evaluator vulnerability to framing.
threats.ruled_out_by: Have annotators audit sampled flipped outputs for preservation of harmful content, with independent labels and adjudication of disagreements.

threats.name: A source-side attack improvement does not transfer to target models
evidence: Breadth Beats Depth: Improving GCG-Based Jailbreak Optimization with Breadth-Oriented Suffix Search
threats.detail: An attack optimized on a source model can improve source ASR while failing on the claimed target models.
threats.ruled_out_by: Evaluate transferred attacks on target models and report target ASR separately from source ASR.

threats.name: An in-loop evaluator changes attack generation as well as scoring
evidence: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
threats.detail: For attacks that query a judge during optimization, changing the judge can alter the attack trajectory, so differences in final ASR do not isolate evaluation quality.
threats.ruled_out_by: Separate fixed-response evaluator comparisons from attack runs; where the evaluator is in-loop, report its effect on generation as part of the result rather than attributing the difference solely to scoring.

threats.name: Attack gains come from more search budget rather than the proposed search strategy
evidence: Breadth Beats Depth: Improving GCG-Based Jailbreak Optimization with Breadth-Oriented Suffix Search
threats.detail: More optimization steps or initial trajectories can produce higher success independently of the claimed search mechanism.
threats.ruled_out_by: Hold the total update or query budget fixed while varying the search strategy, and report the budget used by each baseline.

JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models

baselines.name: Removing non-dictionary items

metrics.name: Attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: ASR depends on the Llama-3-70B judge, whose errors can affect measured success; the authors note that its relatively low false positive rate may systematically reduce reported ASR. They report judge agreement, FPR, and FNR against expert labels alongside the judge-selection evaluation.

metrics.name: Average number of queries
metrics.caveat: Not reported for transfer or hand-crafted attacks because the authors say it is unclear how to count them. For Prompt with RS, the count excludes queries used to optimize the universal prompt template and pre-computed suffix initialization.

metrics.name: Average number of tokens
metrics.caveat: Not reported for transfer or hand-crafted attacks because the authors say it is unclear how to count them. For Prompt with RS, the count excludes optimization of the universal prompt template and pre-computed suffix initialization.

metrics.name: Refusal rate on benign behaviors
metrics.caveat: The authors describe this as a simple sanity check for overly conservative models or defenses, not a substitute for a thorough utility evaluation; some benign behaviors are borderline and providers may disagree about whether they warrant refusal.

metrics.name: Judge agreement
metrics.caveat: Agreement is measured against the majority vote of three expert annotators, whose agreement is approximately 95%; the authors also report false positive and false negative rates.

metrics.name: False positive rate (FPR)
metrics.caveat: Measured against expert majority-vote labels on a set containing benign examples; the authors report agreement and false negative rate alongside it.

metrics.name: False negative rate (FNR)
metrics.caveat: Measured against expert majority-vote labels; the authors report agreement and false positive rate alongside it.

controls.name: Topic-matched benign behaviors
controls.detail: The 100 benign behaviors match the topics of the 100 harmful behaviors and are used to measure refusal rates for models and defenses.
controls.rules_out: That apparent defense effectiveness is simply due to broadly refusing benign requests or detecting topic-related keywords.

controls.name: Un-defended target model
controls.detail: For defense evaluation, transfer attack strings found on an undefended LLM are reused against that same LLM with a defense applied; undefended ASRs are also reported.
controls.rules_out: That the defended-versus-undefended difference is attributable only to using different target models or different attack strings.

controls.name: Benign XS-Test examples in judge evaluation
controls.detail: 100 benign XS-Test examples are included alongside harmful prompt-response examples when evaluating candidate jailbreak judges.
controls.rules_out: That a judge’s apparent performance on harmful examples masks false positives on benign but similar examples.

confounds.name: The chosen judge misclassifies responses, so measured ASR reflects judge error rather than jailbreak success
confounds.detail: The authors note the subjective nature of judging objectionable content and that judge errors can shift reported attack success rates.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare six candidate judges against majority-vote labels from three experts on 200 jailbreak prompt-response pairs and 100 benign XS-Test examples, reporting agreement, FPR, and FNR; they select Llama-3-70B and prohibit benchmark submissions from using it to reduce overfitting.

confounds.name: Defense results look strong because the attacks are transfer attacks, not attacks adapted to the defense
confounds.detail: A defense may appear effective against strings found on an undefended model even if an attacker tailored to that defense would succeed; the authors explicitly call transfer evaluation a simple, non-adaptive evaluation and say it gives only a lower bound on worst-case ASR.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in the reported defense evaluation; the authors state that more sophisticated adaptive attacks could increase ASR.

confounds.name: Lower ASR under a defense is caused by over-refusal rather than selective jailbreak resistance
confounds.detail: A defense that refuses benign requests indiscriminately could appear to reduce attack success.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure refusal rates on 100 topic-matched benign behaviors for Vicuna and Llama-2, with Llama-3 8B as the refusal judge.

confounds.name: Differences in attack performance across behavior sources reflect dataset composition rather than a general attack difference
confounds.detail: The authors note that source-level deviations may arise from imbalances in category composition.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They report ASRs across dataset sources in Appendix B and state that attack ASRs are relatively consistent across sources, with deviations most likely due to category-composition imbalances.

evidence_standards.name: Deterministic decoding for model evaluations
evidence_standards.detail: The framework uses greedy deterministic sampling (temperature 0) and, by default, generates 150 tokens per input.

evidence_standards.name: Expert annotation for judge evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: Three experts label each prompt-response pair; the majority vote is ground truth, and annotator agreement is reported as approximately 95%.

datasets.name: HarmBench classifier validation set
datasets.eval_protocol: 596 behavior–generation pairs; human-majority labels from three annotators are the reference. Standard and contextual behaviors use HarmBench’s corresponding prompts. Generations are truncated to their first 512 tokens before scoring. The white-box GCG evaluation separately uses 30 standard behaviors with baseline harmful probability above 0.9, with the body truncated to 200 tokens.

baselines.name: cais/HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls
baselines.fair_comparison: Scored on the same HarmBench validation pairs and against the same human-majority labels as the LLM judges; all judges run in 4-bit on one NVIDIA T4. The classifier uses its official standard and contextual prompts.

baselines.name: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
baselines.fair_comparison: Scored on the same HarmBench validation pairs and against the same human-majority labels as the classifier and other LLM judges; all judges run in 4-bit on one NVIDIA T4. LLM judges receive the paper’s rubric.

baselines.name: Phi-3.5-mini-instruct
baselines.fair_comparison: Scored on the same HarmBench validation pairs and against the same human-majority labels as the classifier and other LLM judges; all judges run in 4-bit on one NVIDIA T4. LLM judges receive the paper’s rubric.

baselines.name: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
baselines.fair_comparison: Scored on the same HarmBench validation pairs and against the same human-majority labels as the classifier and other LLM judges; all judges run in 4-bit on one NVIDIA T4. LLM judges receive the paper’s rubric.

baselines.name: Greedy search over a fixed library of wrappers
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with GCG on the dedicated classifier; the paper reports the greedy search result on 15 cases and contrasts it with GCG on 30 confident true positives, so the sample sizes differ.

metrics.name: Precision
metrics.caveat: The classifier’s lower precision means it flags some benign content and can inflate ASR; the paper reports recall and other agreement metrics alongside it, and recommends precision-corrected ASR.

metrics.name: Recall
metrics.caveat: The LLM judges’ recall is low and varies substantially across the three models; precision correction does not fix this. The paper reports precision and the other agreement metrics alongside recall.

metrics.name: Flip rate
metrics.caveat: A judge flip could reflect removal of the harm rather than a fooled judge; the paper audits 80 sampled flips for harm preservation. The paper also notes that two LLM-judge rates use small true-positive sets (16 and 47), and that the 30-case, 50-step GCG result is a lower bound on classifier vulnerability.

metrics.name: ASR corrected for judge precision
metrics.caveat: The paper says precision correction does not address the LLM judges’ dominant problem of low, unstable recall; it recommends reporting corrected ASR alongside raw ASR.

metrics.name: Raw annotator agreement
metrics.caveat: The paper does not report Cohen’s kappa because the audit labels are nearly constant, making kappa uninformative; it reports raw agreement and adjudicates disagreements instead.

controls.name: Unwrapped harmful response
controls.detail: The harmful body without an added wrapper is the reference for the wrapper flip-rate comparisons; wrapper conditions add benign framing while leaving the body verbatim.
controls.rules_out: That the reported flips are simply the judge’s original verdicts rather than changes associated with adding a wrapper.

confounds.name: A flip reflects harm removal rather than the judge being fooled
confounds.detail: If the added text removed or neutralized the harmful content, a changed judge verdict would not demonstrate a judge failure on preserved harm.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Two annotators independently labeled a random sample of 80 flipped responses; disagreements were adjudicated, and all 80 were judged to retain harmful content.

confounds.name: Quantization, rather than the released classifier’s behavior, affects the results
confounds.detail: All judges run in 4-bit, so quantization could explain classifier predictions or robustness results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The 4-bit classifier reproduces the benchmark’s stored predictions on 98.7% of items.

confounds.name: The human audit’s harm-preservation result is due to annotator unreliability
confounds.detail: Annotators might fail to recognize harmful content or be misled by the benign framing, weakening the audit’s support for the flips being judge failures.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Annotators completed a calibration round; harmful-control recall was 12/12 and 11/12. They agreed on 75/80 audit items, and all five disagreements were adjudicated as still containing harmful content.

confounds.name: Low LLM-judge recall is caused by the rubric wording rather than the models
confounds.detail: The paper did not tune LLM-judge prompts, so prompt wording may contribute to the observed low recall.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in this study: prompts were not tuned and no prompt-sensitivity experiment was run. The paper notes that refusal-prefix fragility is consistent across the tested models and identifies prompt-sensitivity analysis as future work.

evidence_standards.name: GCG flip-rate uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: For 21 flips among 30 confident true positives, the paper reports a 95% confidence interval of 54%–86%; it does not specify the interval method.

evidence_standards.name: Human audit size and agreement
evidence_standards.detail: Two annotators independently labeled 80 sampled flips after calibration, without seeing each other’s labels; raw agreement was 75/80 (93.8%), and all disagreements were adjudicated. The paper reports raw agreement rather than Cohen’s kappa.

evidence_standards.name: Judge inference and hardware setting
evidence_standards.detail: All judges run in 4-bit on one NVIDIA T4. LLM-judge labels use the first generated token; harmful probabilities use the Yes/No logits. The paper does not report multiple seeds or runs, a statistical test for judge differences, or a general variance-reporting rule.

datasets.name: SorryBENCH
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate human-labeled responses grouped into six response categories; run each LLM-based classifier with three seeds and report average MAE against human labels. The paper reports confidence intervals in Appendix D.1.

datasets.name: StrongREJECT
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate human-labeled responses; run each LLM-based classifier with three seeds and report average MAE against human scores. Report F1 with jailbreak as the positive class; binary decisions use majority vote for the reconstruction game and StrongREJECT rubric score >0.5.

datasets.name: HarmBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate human-labeled responses; run each LLM-based classifier with three seeds and report average MAE against human scores. Report F1 with jailbreak as the positive class; binary decisions use majority vote for the reconstruction game and StrongREJECT rubric score >0.5.

datasets.name: AdvBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Run PAIR, PAP, I-GCG, SlotGCG, and HERETIC against Qwen2-7B-Instruct. For each evaluator LLM, use a separate attack run; report ASR from each classifier’s binary decisions. PAIR requires an in-loop judge, so prefix matching is not used for PAIR.

baselines.name: vanilla LLM-as-a-judge
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside the proposed game using the same three judge LLMs; LLM-based classifiers are run with three seeds on the human-labeled benchmarks.

baselines.name: StrongREJECT rubric
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside the proposed game using the same three judge LLMs; LLM-based classifiers are run with three seeds on the human-labeled benchmarks. The authors set the binary-decision threshold to a rubric score above 0.5 because the original rubric defines no threshold.

metrics.name: MAE
metrics.caveat: MAE can reward a classifier that rarely labels a jailbreak when positive examples are rare; the paper also reports F1, with jailbreak as the positive class.

metrics.name: ASR
metrics.caveat: Reported ASR depends heavily on the classifier and judging LLM; for attacks requiring an in-loop judge, that judge also shapes the attack run. The paper reports ASR by classifier and judge LLM, including the spread across LLMs and original-evaluator ASRs where available.

controls.name: reconstruction-only judge
controls.detail: A preliminary condition uses reconstruction without decoys. The paper reports that it produced 7.2% more false negatives than the StrongREJECT rubric, while the full game produced 30–66% fewer.
controls.rules_out: That reconstruction alone, without the decoy-comparison stage, has the same reported false-negative advantage as the full game.

controls.name: degraded decoys
controls.detail: An ablation varies decoy quality; the paper reports that degrading the decoys leaves refusal handling unchanged but makes the game less conservative.
controls.rules_out: That the game’s conservatism is unaffected by decoy quality.

confounds.name: Direct copying or restating a request can look like fulfillment
confounds.detail: A refusal may repeat the original request and thereby allow reconstruction even though the response did not answer it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The reconstruction is instructed to extract only substantive content provided, excluding content merely restated, named, or refused; the paper measures errors and the fulfillment–recoverability gap on non-fulfilling SorryBENCH response categories, including refusal categories.

confounds.name: Recoverability is not the same as harmful fulfillment
confounds.detail: A non-fulfilling response may reveal the request, while a fulfilling but incomplete response may not reveal enough to reconstruct it; either case can make the game’s decision differ from true attack success.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures the fulfillment–recoverability gap by response category, reporting false-positive-related β for non-fulfilling categories and α plus unrecoverable-response error for fulfilling categories. It acknowledges that incomplete fulfilling responses remain a source of false negatives.

confounds.name: Evaluator choice also changes attack generation, not just evaluation
confounds.detail: For attacks using an in-loop judge, differences in reported ASR may arise partly because the judge shapes the attack trajectory, rather than solely because classifiers score fixed responses differently.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper runs each attack with a separate evaluator-LLM instance and explicitly states that the reported ASR reflects both the judge’s effect on the attack and its evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: Three seeds for LLM-based classifier evaluations; report averages, spreads, and 95% confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: The SorryBENCH, StrongREJECT, and HarmBench evaluations run each LLM-based classifier with three seeds. The paper reports average MAE, spread across LLMs, and 95% confidence intervals for benchmark results; it specifies no statistical significance test or minimum difference threshold.

datasets.name: VENOM
datasets.eval_protocol: Paper-constructed benchmark from real-world knowledge sources in Drug Operations, Explosives & Firearms, and Financial Fraud. Evaluates the full question set using open-ended, multiple-choice, and true/false judgment questions; no train/test split is specified. Each multiple-choice question is presented three times with shuffled option order and is correct only if all three answers are correct. Temperature and Direct/Reason prompting are varied.

datasets.name: AdvBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 50 representative harmful behaviors as seeds for counterfactual planning; each seed is mapped to three benign planning tasks, for 150 tasks total. Task Completion and Logic Coherence are scored by Claude-3.7-sonnet.

baselines.name: GPT-4o
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2.5-32B, and Qwen2.5-7B on the same task sets; knowledge evaluations use the stated temperature and prompt-style conditions.

baselines.name: DeepSeek-V3
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-32B, and Qwen2.5-7B on the same task sets; knowledge evaluations use the stated temperature and prompt-style conditions.

baselines.name: Qwen2.5-32B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Qwen2.5-7B on the same task sets; knowledge evaluations use the stated temperature and prompt-style conditions.

baselines.name: Qwen2.5-7B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Qwen2.5-32B on the same task sets; knowledge evaluations use the stated temperature and prompt-style conditions.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with J1–J4 on the same constructed harmful Q&A samples and replacement-ratio conditions.

metrics.name: Attack Success Rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: The paper says ASR is inherently ambiguous because jailbreak outputs may reflect hallucination, intent obscuration, or style imitation; it instead evaluates harmful-knowledge possession, planning, and judgment.

metrics.name: Keyword Recall (Recall_K)
metrics.caveat: The paper reports that higher temperature slightly increases recall but at the cost of accuracy, so it reports recall alongside other knowledge measures.

metrics.name: Multiple-choice Accuracy (Acc_M)
metrics.caveat: Reason prompting can produce overconfident hallucinations in multiple-choice questions. The paper also reports the proportions correct on all three trials and correct on at least one trial to distinguish reliable from potential knowledge.

metrics.name: Judgment Accuracy (Acc_J)
metrics.caveat: Similar, limited accuracy across models does not show reliable separation of real from fabricated harmful information; the paper also tests judge robustness by progressively replacing factual content.

metrics.name: False Positive Rate (FPR_J)
metrics.caveat: It measures how often a judge flags answers with malicious tone but no factual harmful knowledge; the paper reports it across judge frameworks and tests detection as factual content is progressively removed.

controls.name: Fully replaced factual content with malicious tone preserved
controls.detail: For judge robustness testing, factual harmful content is replaced with misinformation up to the 0% factual-content condition while the malicious tone in the prefix and suffix is kept fixed.
controls.rules_out: If judges still flag these samples, factual harmful knowledge is not necessary for the positive judgment; the result is consistent with judgments driven by malicious tone.

confounds.name: Jailbreak success reflects hallucination or style imitation rather than authentic harmful knowledge
confounds.detail: A high jailbreak success rate could occur without the model possessing accurate, operationally actionable criminal knowledge; the paper explicitly identifies hallucination, intent obscuration, and style imitation as possible explanations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate knowledge grounded in collected real-world sources using open-ended keyword recall, multiple-choice factual questions, and true/false verification questions.

confounds.name: Judge positives reflect toxic language patterns rather than authentic harmful content
confounds.detail: A judge could classify an answer as a jailbreak because of its malicious tone even when its factual harmful content is absent.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Progressively replace factual content while holding malicious tone fixed, including a fully replaced condition, and measure judge false-positive rates and detection across replacement ratios.

evidence_standards.name: Knowledge results reported as average with standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The knowledge evaluation table reports average scores with standard deviation; the paper does not specify seeds, confidence intervals, or a significance test.

evidence_standards.name: Three repeated multiple-choice trials with shuffled options
evidence_standards.detail: Each question is presented three times with option order shuffled, and counts as correct only when the model selects the correct answer in all three trials.

evidence_standards.name: Reported decoding and prompting conditions
evidence_standards.detail: Knowledge results are reported at temperature 0.0 and 0.7, with Direct and Reason prompting; the paper does not state a single decoding condition as the sole basis for results.

evidence_standards.name: Counterfactual planning scores judged by Claude-3.7-sonnet
evidence_standards.detail: Task Completion Score and Logic Coherence Score are evaluated by Claude-3.7-sonnet; no statistical test or uncertainty estimate for these scores is specified.

datasets.name: HarmBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for jailbreak defenses. For RPO, followed the original work’s evaluation protocol and tested RL-based and gradient-based attacks; Circuit Breakers was also tested on HarmBench with the RL attack. No split or trial count is stated.

datasets.name: AgentDojo
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for prompt-injection defenses, including Spotlighting and Prompt Sandwiching with the benchmark’s static attacks and adaptive search attack, and MetaSecAlign in the same agentic setting with the search attack. No split or trial count is stated.

datasets.name: OpenPromptInject
datasets.eval_protocol: Named as a non-agentic prompt-injection benchmark used depending on the defense; this text does not specify the paper’s evaluation protocol on it.

datasets.name: adversarial Davinci
datasets.eval_protocol: Named as a non-agentic prompt-injection benchmark used depending on the defense; this text does not specify the paper’s evaluation protocol on it.

baselines.name: benchmark static attacks
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with adaptive attacks on the same defenses and benchmarks where stated; the paper does not give a common protocol across defenses.

metrics.name: attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: Model-based safety classifiers used as auto-raters can be unreliable and vulnerable to adversarial examples or reward hacking; the authors manually verified all attacks to check that they did not exploit weaknesses in the scoring mechanism.

metrics.name: false positive rate
metrics.caveat: Detectors may need a significantly higher false positive rate on benign data to flag triggers that look benign; the paper reports detector false-positive results and notes they are already higher for these defenses than for the others.

controls.name: same target model without the defense
controls.detail: The paper compares defended models with the same models without the defense; for Data Sentinel, it also compares malicious-task accuracy with an undefended model.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported attack outcomes or task performance require the defense to be present; the paper reports no measurable difference in attack types for the prompting defenses and says Data Sentinel results are comparable to an undefended model.

confounds.name: apparent attack success may exploit weaknesses in the scoring mechanism
confounds.detail: A model-based auto-rater may be fooled, making reported ASR appear high without the attack genuinely succeeding.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors manually verified all attacks to ensure they were not exploiting scoring weaknesses.

confounds.name: detector bypass may not actually redirect the target to the adversarial task
confounds.detail: A detector could be bypassed without the model carrying out the attacker’s intended alternative task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For Data Sentinel, they measured accuracy on the malicious task for sentiment-analysis and spam-detection trials and report over 80% accuracy on both.

evidence_standards.name: human red-teaming study size
evidence_standards.detail: The online red-teaming competition had over 500 participants; the paper does not state a statistical test, variance estimate, or seed-based decision rule.

datasets.name: Forbidden question dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: 160 questions across 16 violation categories (10 per category; Child Endangerment excluded). Questions were selected from prior work and generated with a designed prompt, then filtered for improper, duplicate, or irrelevant items and manually screened; two annotators reviewed each question. No split is stated. Each question was attacked individually with each method on each target LLM. ASR is the fraction of successful queries, judged by GPT-4-Turbo from three aspects. For most methods, evaluation uses top-1 ASR; GE tests 50 generation settings per question and counts the question successful if any response succeeds.

baselines.name: AIM
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same forbidden questions and target LLMs, using the paper's shared ASR evaluation; no method-specific equalization beyond the stated step settings.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same forbidden questions and target LLMs, using the paper's shared ASR evaluation; no method-specific equalization beyond the stated step settings.

metrics.name: Attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: The paper says automatic ASR evaluation is imperfect and does not assess response quality; it reports GPT-4-Turbo judging from three aspects and human annotation comparing the judge with other evaluation methods.

controls.name: Direct-query baseline (no jailbreak attack)
controls.detail: Query the target LLM with the forbidden question alone.
controls.rules_out: That an attack's measured success is explained solely by the model already answering the forbidden question without a jailbreak.

controls.name: No additional defense
controls.detail: Report attack results without an added defense alongside results with individual defenses and all eight defenses combined.
controls.rules_out: That a measured defense-associated reduction is merely the attack's baseline performance rather than a change under the defense condition.

confounds.name: Jailbreak success labels may be misclassified by the evaluation method
confounds.detail: An apparent ASR difference could reflect weaknesses in string matching or LLM-as-a-judge labeling rather than actual differences in jailbreak success.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors conducted human annotation comparing evaluation approaches and report that their GPT-4-Turbo judge, which labels responses from three aspects, outperformed the other methods; they acknowledge that automatic evaluation remains imperfect.

confounds.name: Bias in the constructed questions or LLM-assisted attack process
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that LLM involvement in constructing forbidden-question datasets and assisting some attacks could introduce unknown biases, making observed results reflect those biases rather than attack performance more generally.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Questions were manually screened and reviewed by two annotators, and the authors report manual checks and modifications; they explicitly concede that these steps may not remove all bias.

evidence_standards.name: Attack evaluation and decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: For all methods except GE, report top-1 ASR. For each GE candidate question, generate one response with the highest likelihood for each of 50 generation settings; count the question successful if any response is labeled successful. The maximum prompt-modification count is 50 per question, while GCG and COLD use 500 gcg_step optimization steps. The paper does not report seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: JailbreakBench
datasets.eval_protocol: 100 distinct harmful behaviors; evaluate against its GCG, PAIR, and hand-crafted JBC attacks on the reported models, using benchmark-default attack and defense settings. Report ASR; Table 1 says prompts and responses are classified using Llama Guard. No evaluation split or trial count is stated.

datasets.name: HarmBench
datasets.eval_protocol: 400 text-based harmful behaviors; evaluate against six selected text attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, TAP, Few-Shot, PAP) out of 18, chosen for highest average ASR, on the reported models. Report ASR using the benchmark's LLM-as-a-judge evaluation; use default attack and defense settings. No evaluation split or trial count is stated.

datasets.name: MT-Bench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate models with and without RPO on multiturn interaction; report the benchmark score. No split, trial count, or further scoring details are stated.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate models with and without RPO on domain knowledge; report the benchmark score. No split, trial count, or further scoring details are stated.

controls.name: Unmodified model / no defense
controls.detail: The base or None condition is reported alongside RPO in the attack and benign-use evaluations.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported change is attributable to adding RPO rather than being present in the model without the defense.

confounds.name: RPO reduces ASR by damaging general or benign capability, rather than by improving jailbreak robustness
confounds.detail: A drop in attack success could arise if the defended model performs worse generally or rejects benign requests.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate with and without RPO on MT-Bench and MMLU, and assess benign prompts for unnecessary refusals; the paper reports a small MT-Bench reduction, negligible MMLU reduction, and no unnecessary rejection on benign prompts.

datasets.name: JailbreakBench
datasets.eval_protocol: 100 harmful questions; reports attack success rate (ASR), the proportion of attempts eliciting a harmful response. Harmfulness is judged by majority vote from BeaverDam, WildGuard, and Llama Guard4. Also used for position and semantic-relatedness ablations; the position ablation uses 7-batch prompts.

datasets.name: StrongREJECT
datasets.eval_protocol: 313 harmful questions; reports ASR, with harmfulness judged by majority vote from BeaverDam, WildGuard, and Llama Guard4.

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as semantically unrelated benign math questions in batch prompts for semantic-relatedness and refusal-signal analyses; the excerpt does not specify a split or item count.

datasets.name: Alpaca
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as harmless single prompts for the refusal-score comparison; the excerpt does not specify a split or item count.

baselines.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with DPO after both are trained on a 500-example dataset in 5-batch format using LoRA.

metrics.name: Attack Success Rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: Harmfulness judgments may depend on a single evaluator; the paper instead uses majority vote from BeaverDam, WildGuard, and Llama Guard4, and reports judge-validation agreement analysis with GPT-5.3.

metrics.name: Reward gap (ΔR)
metrics.caveat: The open-source reward models are proxies and may not capture the target models’ actual alignment signals; the paper checks for consistent trends across multiple open-source reward models.

controls.name: No attack / single harmful prompt
controls.detail: Evaluates the harmful question in isolation alongside batch-prompting conditions.
controls.rules_out: That the observed harmful responses are simply due to the harmful questions being answerable even without batch composition.

controls.name: SFT exposure condition
controls.detail: Trains on batch-structured inputs with ideal responses using the same 500-example, 5-batch LoRA setup as DPO, but without explicitly reinforcing the safe-versus-unsafe preference margin.
controls.rules_out: That merely exposing the model to batch-structured examples is sufficient to explain DPO’s mitigation.

controls.name: Semantically related benign questions
controls.detail: Compares batches using related benign questions with batches using unrelated GSM8K questions.
controls.rules_out: That attack effectiveness requires benign context semantically related to the harmful question.

controls.name: Benign batch prompts after DPO
controls.detail: Checks utility on benign batch prompts after DPO training; the paper reports that utility is largely preserved.
controls.rules_out: That DPO’s lower ASR is merely caused by rejecting batch inputs wholesale.

confounds.name: The vulnerability is an in-context-learning effect
confounds.detail: The apparent batch-prompting success could instead come from harmful question–answer demonstrations teaching the model to answer harmfully.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Batch prompting uses questions without answer demonstrations; the paper compares it with ICL attacks, reporting 55% ASR for batch prompting versus 0% for ICL at 128 shots on Llama-3.1-8B.

confounds.name: The vulnerability is a long-context effect
confounds.detail: The apparent attack success could be caused simply by longer input context.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports 55% ASR for batch prompting at an average of 906 tokens versus 40% for a long-context attack at 6,654 tokens, and reports an additional experiment scaling batch size to extreme values.

confounds.name: Batch-prompting preference-signal degradation is only a format artifact
confounds.detail: The reward-gap change might reflect the batch template’s format rather than a degraded safety preference signal.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says Appendix B.3 provides additional analyses showing the degradation is not a format-level artifact; the specific measurements are not given in the supplied text.

confounds.name: Mitigation works merely because the model had rarely seen batch inputs during alignment
confounds.detail: If unfamiliarity with batch structure caused the vulnerability, exposure to batch examples alone could account for mitigation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: SFT exposes the model to batch-structured examples but mitigates less than DPO, which explicitly reinforces the preference margin between safe and unsafe responses.

confounds.name: DPO reduces ASR through general capability loss or blanket refusal
confounds.detail: A lower ASR could result from refusing benign batch questions as well as harmful ones.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that utility on benign batch prompts is largely preserved after DPO.

confounds.name: Open-source reward models do not represent the target models’ actual alignment signals
confounds.detail: The reward-gap analysis may not reflect the inaccessible reward models used to align the target LLMs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports consistent trends across multiple open-source reward models, while acknowledging that these proxies may not fully capture each target model’s internal alignment signal.

confounds.name: Automatic jailbreak-success judging may misclassify responses
confounds.detail: ASR depends on labeling responses as successful or unsuccessful, so the reported result could reflect judge errors rather than actual jailbreak success.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses GPT-4-Turbo to judge responses on three aspects and reports a human-annotation comparison in which its method outperforms string matching and other LLM-as-a-judge methods.

evidence_standards.name: Reported response-generation and success-counting rule
evidence_standards.detail: For attacks other than GE, report top-1 ASR using a single highest-likelihood response for each jailbreak candidate prompt. For GE, test 50 generation settings per forbidden question and count the question as successfully jailbroken if any response is labeled successful. The paper does not report a statistical test, repeated-seed rule, or variance-based threshold for deciding whether differences are real.

datasets.eval_protocol: 100 harmful requests; evaluated on five open-source target models under the main B=10 target-model-query comparison. Scored with HarmBench ASR and StrongREJECT mean score. No split or preprocessing is specified.

baselines.fair_comparison: All methods use Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 as attacker LLM, a maximum target response length of 512 tokens, and the same B=10 target-model-query budget in the main comparison; the paper evaluates the first 10 queries from longer attack trajectories.

metrics.name: HarmBench attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that automated evaluators can overestimate attack success by rewarding superficial compliance; it reports StrongREJECT mean score alongside ASR and says both evaluators are independent of the methods’ in-loop judges.

confounds.name: Apparent attack success may be superficial compliance or evaluator overestimation
confounds.detail: A judge may count a response as a successful jailbreak even when it only appears compliant, making reported ASR look high without substantive fulfillment of the harmful request.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate with HarmBench ASR and the StrongREJECT fine-tuned evaluator’s mean score, which assesses the extent of useful information in responses; the paper states both evaluators are independent of the compared methods’ in-loop judges.

datasets.name: AdvBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Simulation: a subset of 500 high-risk prompts; malicious and CMPE responses were scored 10 times per judge, normalized to [0,1], and averaged per prompt-response pair. Malicious-response quality control used five evaluations by each of six judges; 453 samples met the average-score-above-0.75 criterion on at least four judges, and the remaining 47 were manually modified and retested. End-to-end runs used the first 50 adversarial goals, the same goal set across frameworks; PAIR and GPTFuzz had a maximum of 50 iterations per prompt, and AutoDAN-Turbo a maximum of 20 epochs. End-to-end ASR is validated true positives divided by total prompts.

baselines.name: Detect-and-block
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with detect-and-misdirect using the same attack frameworks, goal sets, victim models, attack budgets, and LLaMA-Guard-3-8B defense judge; detected harmful responses are replaced with refusal rather than CMPE responses.

metrics.name: Attacker success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: Attacker-claimed positive exits can be false positives, including CMPE misdirection accepted as successful; end-to-end ASR is therefore reported as validated true positives divided by total prompts, with FP and MI-FP outcomes also distinguished. Simulation results are estimated ASR upper bounds, averaged over 500 per-sample bounds.

metrics.name: Judge false-negative rate (FN)
metrics.caveat: Estimated from direct malicious responses, which the paper says provide a conservative estimate relative to obfuscated or role-play attack responses; the estimate uses the complement of the average normalized judge score.

metrics.name: Misdirection-induced false-positive rate (MI-FP)
metrics.caveat: Estimated from CMPE response scores as the average normalized judge output per prompt-response pair; this is a judge-based estimate, not verification that the response is harmful.

metrics.name: Positive exits, negative exits, FP, MI-FP, and TP
metrics.caveat: A positive exit is not necessarily a genuine attack success; positive exits were independently classified, and non-CMPE responses counted as TP only if genuinely harmful and actionable.

metrics.name: Average iterations / average epochs
metrics.caveat: Fewer iterations can reflect premature termination on MI-FPs rather than improved attack efficiency; the paper reports exit types and validated ASR alongside these averages.

controls.name: Detect-and-block condition
controls.detail: For the same attack frameworks, goals, victim models, budgets, and defense judge, detected harmful responses receive a refusal instead of a CMPE response.
controls.rules_out: That the observed difference is explained merely by running the attack and defense setup, rather than replacing predictable refusals with CMPE misdirection.

confounds.name: Positive exits could be mistaken for genuine harmful attack success
confounds.detail: The attacker’s judge may accept safe or invalid responses, including controlled CMPE responses, so attacker-reported success could look high without harmful output.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Final-response validation: two independent judges classified positive exits as FP or TP, disagreements were manually inspected, and CMPE exits were recorded as MI-FPs after confirming the controlled response contained no harmful output.

confounds.name: Fewer iterations could indicate improved attack efficiency rather than disruption by misdirection
confounds.detail: A reduction in iterations alone could make CMPE appear effective even if it had not disrupted the attack’s search or prevented genuine success.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports positive and negative exits, MI-FP/FP/TP counts, and validated ASR alongside average iterations or epochs; it interprets early termination as MI-FP termination rather than improved attack efficiency.

confounds.name: Misdirection may confuse benign human users
confounds.detail: The authors note that misdirection responses could have collateral effects in chatbot settings, where benign users may need clear refusals or policy explanations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper states that it did not conduct a dedicated study of collateral effects on benign human users.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated judge scoring for simulation estimates
evidence_standards.detail: Each of 500 prompts had paired malicious and CMPE responses evaluated 10 times per judge; the 10 normalized outputs were averaged per prompt-response pair, and ASR bounds were computed per sample and averaged over 500 samples. No statistical test or uncertainty threshold is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Manual quality control and final-response validation
evidence_standards.detail: Malicious responses were evaluated five times by each of six judges, with the stated score criterion and manual modification/retesting for the remaining samples. For end-to-end positive exits, two judges independently classified outcomes and disagreements were resolved by manual inspection.
