metrics.caveat: The authors describe the automated checks as rudimentary and say they yield poor accuracy; they can miss misalignment, such as syntactically valid code that does not follow the task. The paper also reports GPT-4-based evaluations and manual evaluations.

metrics.name: GPT-4-based property-test jailbreak success
metrics.caveat: GPT-4 can itself be jailbroken, and its judgments can mistake an attack for the original task. The paper compares it with programmatic tests and reports manual evaluations; it notes the methods have complementary blind spots.

metrics.name: manual misalignment rate and jailbreak-intent success rate
metrics.caveat: Partial task or intent alignment can cause annotator disagreement. The paper reports separate misalignment and intent-satisfaction labels, defines strict attack success as intent satisfaction with at least partial task misalignment, and reports inter-annotator agreement.

metrics.name: inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ)
metrics.caveat: Annotators disagreed in cases of partial task or intent misalignment; disagreements were resolved by a third annotator. The paper reports κ = 0.6 over both labels.

metrics.name: GPT-4 true-positive rate and false-negative rate
metrics.caveat: GPT-4 evaluations do not match human judgments perfectly; the paper uses these rates against manual evaluations to scale GPT-4 results.

confounds.name: apparent jailbreak success reflects limitations of the automated property tests rather than actual task misalignment
confounds.detail: The authors note that simple functional checks can miss misaligned outputs—for example, syntactically valid code that ignores the requested task could pass a code well-formedness check.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They also evaluate with GPT-4 and conduct manual evaluations; they compare programmatic and GPT-4 results and report that the methods have complementary blind spots.

confounds.name: apparent success or failure in GPT-4 evaluation reflects the evaluator itself being jailbroken or misled
confounds.detail: The paper reports that GPT-4 was occasionally jailbroken and could be led to treat an attack instruction as the original task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare GPT-4 judgments with programmatic tests, perform manual evaluations, and scale GPT-4 results using its true-positive and false-negative rates against the manual evaluations; the authors still acknowledge that detection remains brittle.

evidence_standards.name: manual annotation procedure
evidence_standards.detail: Human evaluation sampled 800 jailbreaks across four models. Each prompt was independently labeled by two annotators, with disagreements resolved by a third; the reported inter-annotator agreement was κ = 0.6 over both labels. Reported figures are rounded to the nearest integer. The paper does not specify seeds, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or a statistical significance test.

evidence_standards.name: Two-author independent screening and extraction
evidence_standards.detail: Both authors independently screened Tier-1 and Tier-2 candidates and extracted core corpus fields; disagreements were resolved by discussion. No external tie-breaker was used, and the review reports no statistical test or inferential threshold for deciding that differences are real.

datasets.name: GuidedBench
datasets.eval_protocol: 200 curated harmful-question cases: 180 core cases and 20 additional cases. Evaluate ten jailbreak methods on five victim LLMs; additional topics are model-specific. Take the first 512 tokens of each jailbreak response using the Llama tokenizer. Each case is independently scored by GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Doubao-v1.5-pro; reported LLM-based scores use DeepSeek-V3. GuidedEval ASR averages each case’s equal-weighted scoring-point completion rate across questions.

metrics.name: ASR (GuidedEval generalized ASR)
metrics.caveat: Prior evaluation systems can overestimate success for incomplete or misunderstood harmful responses, and underestimate it when disclaimers or irrelevant content interfere. GuidedEval instead reports the equal-weighted completion rate of case-specific guideline scoring points, using binary semantic matches.

metrics.name: False positive rate (FPR)
metrics.caveat: Measured on a filtered subset of objectively identifiable failure cases, so it characterizes those failure modes rather than all responses.

metrics.name: Evaluator-score variance
metrics.caveat: Higher variance indicates less consistent scores across evaluators; the paper reports average variance across evaluation systems.

metrics.name: Shannon entropy (H) and normalized entropy (H_norm)
metrics.caveat: Calculated on effective scores (scores > 0); reported to assess use of the scoring spectrum and alongside score distributions.

metrics.name: Human–LLM agreement rate
metrics.caveat: Human annotations are not an absolute gold standard; the paper reports agreement with two expert annotators and notes their limitations on complex or ambiguous cases.

metrics.name: Coefficient of variation across victim LLMs and topics
metrics.caveat: Captures method dependence on victim models or topics; the paper also reports variance decomposition analysis.

controls.name: Victim LLM with no jailbreak applied
controls.detail: The dataset construction checks that core questions are refused by the corresponding victim LLMs without an attack.
controls.rules_out: That harmful questions are answered readily without a jailbreak, supporting attribution of harmful responses to the attack condition.

confounds.name: Apparent jailbreak success is due to evaluators accepting objectively failed responses
confounds.detail: Responses that misunderstand the question, provide only general advice, contain invalid rephrasing or garbled text, or otherwise fail can still be classified as successful.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Filter responses into five identifiable failure-mode subsets and measure each evaluation system’s FPR on them.

confounds.name: Evaluator-model choice, rather than the evaluation system, drives score differences
confounds.detail: Different LLM evaluators may score the same responses inconsistently, making results dependent on the chosen judge.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Have three evaluator LLMs independently score each case and compare repeated-score variance across evaluation systems.

confounds.name: LLM judge scores do not reflect human judgments
confounds.detail: Agreement between LLM evaluators could be mistaken for reliable evaluation even if their judgments diverge from human annotations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare LLM judgments with annotations from two domain experts on a random sample of 700 instances; the paper also cautions that human labels are not an absolute gold standard.

confounds.name: A nominally multi-value evaluation system effectively gives only binary scores
confounds.detail: Extreme or bimodal scores could make apparent scoring granularity uninformative.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare score distributions and calculate Shannon and normalized entropy for effective scores.

evidence_standards.name: Three independent evaluator LLMs per case; report evaluator variance
evidence_standards.detail: Each case is scored independently by GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Doubao-v1.5-pro to assess consistency. The paper reports average variance across evaluation systems; its reported LLM-based scores use DeepSeek-V3.

evidence_standards.name: Human validation study
evidence_standards.detail: Two domain experts independently annotated 700 randomly sampled instances. The sample was designed for a 99% confidence level with a ±5% margin of error; the paper reports human–human and human–LLM agreement rates.

datasets.name: AdvBench
datasets.eval_protocol: 520 harmful instructions total; evaluate attack methods on 510 behaviors, excluding 10 used for training or validation. JSR is the percentage of harmful responses, assessed by GPT-4o.

datasets.name: Self Reminder Data (SRD)
datasets.eval_protocol: 155 jailbreak prompts split into 80 training and 75 test prompts. Pair each test prompt with five distinct AdvBench harmful behaviors to form 375 test samples; evaluate attacks using JSR, with GPT-4o assessing harmful responses.

datasets.name: Xstest
datasets.eval_protocol: 250 safety prompts across ten categories; randomly select 50 for training/reflection and use the remaining 200 for testing. Report the percentage of unjustified rejections, assessed by GPT-4o.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: 14,042 multiple-choice questions; evaluate in a 0-shot chain-of-thought setting and report accuracy.

baselines.name: No defense
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside defense methods on the same defense LLMs and attack sets.

baselines.name: Self Reminder
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same defense LLMs and attack sets; the paper says each baseline follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: Goal Prioritization
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same defense LLMs and attack sets; applied as safety instructions without fine-tuning.

baselines.name: In-Context Defense (ICD)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same defense LLMs and attack sets; the paper says each baseline follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: GCG
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper's AdvBench-based and SRD-based evaluations; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: PAIR
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper's AdvBench-based evaluation; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: In-Context Attack (ICA)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper's AdvBench-based and SRD-based evaluations; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: AutoDAN
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper's AdvBench-based evaluation; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: Combination 2
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper's AdvBench-based and SRD-based evaluations; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: SRD prompts without refinement
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the SRD test samples with the same harmful questions; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: SRD + GCG
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the SRD test samples with the same harmful questions; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: SRD + ICA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the SRD test samples with the same harmful questions; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

baselines.name: SRD + Combination 2
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the SRD test samples with the same harmful questions; follows its respective paper's experimental setup.

metrics.name: Jailbreak Success Rate (JSR)
metrics.caveat: A low JSR could accompany excessive refusals; the paper also reports the over-defense rate on Xstest.

controls.name: No-defense model
controls.detail: Evaluate the defense LLM without a defense method, alongside the defended conditions; also compare MMLU accuracy with and without ICAG-5 prompts.
controls.rules_out: Provides an unmodified reference for judging defense effects and whether ICAG prompts change general-task accuracy.

controls.name: ICAG-0
controls.detail: Apply defense directly to the initial prompt set without involving the attack agent, and compare with later ICAG iterations.
controls.rules_out: Whether the iterative attack-agent component contributes beyond applying the initial defense directly.

confounds.name: Lower JSR reflects blanket refusal rather than better jailbreak-specific defense
confounds.detail: A defense could lower harmful responses simply by refusing benign safety prompts too.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure the over-defense rate on Xstest, using GPT-4o to identify unjustified refusals.

confounds.name: General capability damage rather than a targeted safety effect
confounds.detail: ICAG prompts might lower harmful responses by impairing general helpfulness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare MMLU accuracy with no defense and with ICAG-5 system prompts.

confounds.name: Low JSR on Llama models is due to their existing safety alignment, not ICAG
confounds.detail: The paper notes that Llama models have low JSR across defense methods, attributing this to safety alignment from pre-training and instruction fine-tuning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare ICAG with other defense methods on the same Llama models and attack tests; the paper reports ICAG has lower JSR across the tests.

datasets.name: HarmBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates benchmark prompts; reports classifier-based ASR using the HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls classifier. No split or trial count is specified.

datasets.name: JailbreakBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses its harmful-behavior prompts and evaluates responses with Llama-Guard-4-12B, reporting ASR. No split or trial count is specified.

datasets.name: StrongREJECT
datasets.eval_protocol: Follows the StrongREJECT evaluation protocol and reports dataset-level SRS as the average of per-sample scores; rescales SRS from [0, 1] to [0, 100]. No split or trial count is specified.

baselines.name: Zeroshot
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same target dLLMs and benchmarks as RMT-Jailbreak; no further matching details are specified.

baselines.name: GCG
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same target dLLMs and benchmarks as RMT-Jailbreak; no further matching details are specified.

baselines.name: AutoDAN
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same target dLLMs and benchmarks as RMT-Jailbreak; in transfer comparisons, direct AutoDAN and +RMT use the same attack method and target dLLM.

baselines.name: AIM
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same target dLLMs and benchmarks as RMT-Jailbreak; no further matching details are specified.

baselines.name: PAIR
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same target dLLMs and benchmarks as RMT-Jailbreak; no further matching details are specified.

baselines.name: ReNeLLM
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same target dLLMs and benchmarks as RMT-Jailbreak; no further matching details are specified.

baselines.name: DIJA
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same target dLLMs and benchmarks. The paper sets RMT's mask ratio to 0.8 to approximately match DIJA's, and reports actual mask ratios for both.

baselines.name: RA
baselines.fair_comparison: In transfer comparisons, direct RA and +RMT use the same attack method and target dLLM.

metrics.name: ASR
metrics.caveat: A success-rate gain does not necessarily mean responses are more harmful or extreme; the paper reports HS alongside ASR and notes that HS is not uniformly higher.

metrics.name: SRS
metrics.caveat: A gain in jailbreak score does not necessarily mean responses are more harmful or extreme; the paper reports HS alongside SRS and notes that HS is not uniformly higher.

controls.name: direct AR-oriented attack without RMT
controls.detail: Applies the original AR attack directly to the target dLLM, alongside applying RMT to a response induced by that attack.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether gains come from response-mediated transfer rather than merely applying the AR attack to the target dLLM.

controls.name: continuous masking at the same mask ratio
controls.detail: Compares continuous masking with uniform masking while holding the mask ratio fixed.
controls.rules_out: Whether uniform masking's advantage is due simply to the number of visible tokens rather than their distribution.

confounds.name: gains reflect more extreme harmful outputs rather than more reliable jailbreak success
confounds.detail: ASR or SRS could rise because successful outputs are more harmful, rather than because jailbreaks succeed more reliably.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports GPT-4o harmfulness scores alongside ASR/SRS and observes that the gains are not accompanied by uniformly higher HS.

confounds.name: gains are specific to a benchmark or evaluator
confounds.detail: The headline improvement could reflect the particular evaluation benchmark or its evaluator rather than broader attack effectiveness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports results across HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and StrongREJECT, which use different evaluation protocols.

confounds.name: gains come from mask ratio rather than the template construction
confounds.detail: RMT's performance advantage could be explained by differences in how much of the response is masked.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports actual mask ratios for RMT and DIJA; also compares uniform and continuous masking at the same mask ratio.

datasets.name: AdvBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Harmful behaviors are used for plain-prompt and prefill-attack evaluations; the prefill is “Sure, here is,” and refusal is scored by matching a fixed refusal-phrase list. The paper reports sample counts per experiment rather than one common split (including n=100 for several causal tests). A separate content audit uses 200-token generations on 50 prompts per model. For the held-out refuse-state transfer, the state is estimated on 260 prompts and tested on a disjoint 100; for held-out harm-direction restoration, the direction is trained on a disjoint 200-prompt split and tested on 100.

datasets.name: Alpaca
datasets.eval_protocol: Benign instructions are used to train the harm probe and to measure false positives or over-refusal under interventions. In the pre-registered 2×2, Alpaca supplies the benign-clean cell (n=120 per cell for Qwen2.5-1.5B); the paper does not give a general evaluation split or count.

datasets.name: XSTest
datasets.eval_protocol: The safe split supplies benign prompts designed to sound harmful; the unsafe split supplies harmful prompts. The AdvBench-trained harm probe is evaluated on these prompts, including the fraction of safe prompts above the 0.5 threshold and the separation of safe from unsafe prompts. XSTest-safe also supplies the benign-scary cell in the pre-registered 2×2; no split size is specified.

datasets.name: MaliciousInstruct
datasets.eval_protocol: Used with AdvBench as a mixed-source training set for a harm probe; the paper reports that this raises sensitivity but increases XSTest-safe false positives from 12% to 64%. It does not specify a split or trial count.

baselines.name: Qwen2.5-1.5B base
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Qwen2.5-1.5B instruction-tuned under the identical early prefill-edge knockout and mass-matched control; harmful content is scored because the base model has no refusal behavior to restore.

baselines.name: Qwen2.5-7B base
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the instruction-tuned model using the identical early prefill-edge knockout and mass-matched control; harmful content is scored because the base model has no refusal behavior to restore.

metrics.name: Refusal rate
metrics.caveat: A refusal-phrase string match does not establish coherent harmful compliance when no refusal is detected, and can count safe deflections as non-refusals. The paper also reads harmful content directly with a judge-free content rule and checks coherence and deflection.

metrics.name: Harm-probe AUC
metrics.caveat: The probe is calibrated to AdvBench phrasing: it scores differently phrased XSTest-unsafe prompts at 0.49, and mixed-source training raises false positives on XSTest-safe prompts from 12% to 64%. The paper reports the XSTest safe/unsafe results and false-positive rates alongside the AdvBench results.

metrics.name: Behavior AUC
metrics.caveat: Under the strong prefill nearly all prompts comply, leaving little variation; it is undefined when all prompts comply, as for SmolLM2. The paper also reports refusal rates and, for the weakened-prefill split, harm-probe AUC.

metrics.name: Harmful-content rate
metrics.caveat: A content rule can conservatively miss harmful content; the paper manually reads the remaining non-refusals in its audit and reports refusal-string matching and coherence alongside the content score.

metrics.name: Coherence / distinct-token ratio
metrics.caveat: A coherence score alone does not establish that a continuation is harmful compliance. The paper reports harmful-content and refusal scores alongside it.

metrics.name: Single-direction decision AUC
metrics.caveat: The best score is a maximum over layers and generated positions and is therefore post-selection-optimistic. The paper compares it with a full linear probe and reports a bootstrap interval for the capacity gain.

controls.name: Matched-norm orthogonal-random direction
controls.detail: A direction orthogonalized to the harm direction and matched in norm is injected at the same response positions; the refuse-state transfer also has a matched-norm orthogonal-random control.
controls.rules_out: That any perturbation of the same size explains the harm-direction restoration or the refuse-state transfer.

controls.name: Benign-residual patch
controls.detail: The mean benign residual is patched at the same position as the full harmful-residual patch.
controls.rules_out: A harm-specific explanation of the full-residual patch’s 100% refusal restoration; the benign patch produces the same restoration, indicating generic disruption.

controls.name: Dose-matched position conditions
controls.detail: The harm direction is injected over the first half, second half, or whole response at matched per-position dose; onset-only and reduced-strength conditions are also tested.
controls.rules_out: That the effect is due merely to total dose, the whole response, or the onset token; the comparison licenses localization to an early multi-token window.

controls.name: Mass-matched non-prefill attention knockout
controls.detail: The same total baseline attention mass is removed from non-prefill prompt keys as from prefill keys.
controls.rules_out: That refusal recovery is caused by removing attention mass generally rather than by cutting attention to the prefill.

controls.name: Late-window and half-strength attention knockout
controls.detail: The attention knockout is applied in the late response window or at half strength, alongside the early-window knockout.
controls.rules_out: That any attention knockout or any knockout dose produces the early-window effect.

controls.name: Base-model knockout condition
controls.detail: The identical prefill-edge knockout and mass-matched control are run on Qwen2.5-1.5B base and Qwen2.5-7B base models.
controls.rules_out: That the prefill’s early-attention dependence requires safety tuning; the same prefill-specific harmful-content collapse in base models supports generic autoregressive conditioning.

controls.name: Benign prompts under intervention
controls.detail: Harm-direction restoration, refuse-state transfer, and early attention knockout are also tested on benign prompts under the prefill.
controls.rules_out: That the intervention’s apparent benefit is simply broad refusal induction or nonspecific degradation; the comparison measures benign over-refusal alongside harmful refusal.

controls.name: Harm-by-surface 2×2 conditions
controls.detail: The pre-registered comparison includes harmful-scary and harmful-clean prompts and benign-scary and benign-clean prompts; the harmful-scary versus harmful-clean comparison is within AdvBench.
controls.rules_out: That refusal or the harm-probe result is explained solely by trigger-word surface features; the within-AdvBench contrast holds source and register fixed.

controls.name: Benign forced-prefix conditions
controls.detail: Harmful prompts are given a benign non-affirmative prefix (“Here’s a fun fact:”) or a benign affirmative prefix (“Sure, here is a poem about”) for the onset-projection and syntax checks.
controls.rules_out: That a low onset projection identifies refusal displacement, or that affirmative syntax alone explains harmful continuation.

controls.name: Sham and intervention-validation checks
controls.detail: Attention and MLP interventions are checked with sham-hook bit-identity and relevant edge-masking, cache-consistency, faithfulness, and locality tests before behavioral runs.
controls.rules_out: That the reported intervention effect is caused by a faulty hook or an unintended change outside the specified intervention.

confounds.name: The harm probe may read scary vocabulary rather than harm
confounds.detail: A probe trained to distinguish AdvBench from Alpaca could exploit violent or trigger-word surface features, making the reported harm representation misleading.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate the AdvBench-trained probe on XSTest’s scary-sounding safe and unsafe prompts, and use the pre-registered harm-by-surface 2×2; harmful-clean and harmful-scary AdvBench prompts have nearly identical probe scores.

confounds.name: Prompt length or keyword count may explain who refuses under the weakened prefill
confounds.detail: These surface properties could account for the refuse-versus-comply split attributed to harm strength.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On the weakened-prefill split, length and scary-keyword count predict at chance, and the harm-probe AUC remains when length and keyword count are regressed out. The paper notes that topic, severity, and formality are not held fixed.

confounds.name: Full-residual refusal restoration may be generic disruption
confounds.detail: The intervention could break the prefill continuation and make the model revert to refusal regardless of harm content.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Patch the mean benign residual at the same position; it also restores refusal to 100%, so the paper demotes the full-residual result and relies on the controlled harm-direction result instead.

confounds.name: Direction-injection effects may be generic perturbation
confounds.detail: The harm direction’s apparent restoration could result from perturbing the response rather than from the harm direction specifically.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against a matched-norm orthogonal-random direction; the harm-direction restoration exceeds this control, with bootstrap confidence intervals for the difference.

confounds.name: The prefill effect may be safety-specific active suppression rather than generic conditioning
confounds.detail: The early-attention result in an instruction-tuned model could reflect an actively suppressed safety mechanism.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run the identical knockout against a mass-matched control on non-safety-tuned Qwen base models at 1.5B and 7B; the prefill-specific harmful-content collapse also occurs there.

confounds.name: Refusal-string changes may reflect deflection, degeneration, or incoherent output rather than harmful compliance
confounds.detail: A missing refusal phrase could be misread as compliance, or a refusal increase could reflect degraded generation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use a judge-free harmful-content read, a coherence/repetition rule, and a deflection-marker list; manually inspect the audited non-refusals. The paper reports that these reads agree across causal conditions.

confounds.name: The onset projection may measure forced-token content rather than refusal displacement
confounds.detail: The projection onto the harm direction at the forced onset could reflect the content of the prefix token at that position.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare with benign forced prefixes, which produce still-lower onset projections without being the attack; the paper consequently treats the projection as illustrative and relies on positional patching for localization.

confounds.name: The surface coefficient in the 2×2 may be confounded by source and register
confounds.detail: Benign-scary prompts are all XSTest and benign-clean prompts are all Alpaca, so their refusal difference may partly reflect dataset or register rather than surface.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper explicitly does not rule this out for the benign-side surface coefficient; it bases the harm-primary conclusion instead on the within-AdvBench harmful-scary versus harmful-clean comparison.

confounds.name: The harm probe may not generalize across phrasing or sources
confounds.detail: The monitor’s reported detection could depend on AdvBench-style wording rather than source-general harm recognition.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures performance on differently phrased XSTest-unsafe prompts and tests mixed-source training with MaliciousInstruct, but concedes that source-general detection remains unbuilt.

confounds.name: State-transfer restoration may be due to prompt overlap
confounds.detail: The estimated refuse-state could restore refusal only on prompts used to construct it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Estimate the state on a 260-prompt AdvBench training split and test on a disjoint 100-prompt split; also report an in-distribution reference.

confounds.name: An MLP effect may reflect decodability rather than an active safety-specific computation
confounds.detail: A difference-of-means injection can show that a signal is readable or injectable without showing that the MLP pathway actively computes the safety-specific effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use a frozen-residual path patch that routes the prefill counterfactual through the early-MLP sub-block alone, comparing instruct, base, and mass-matched conditions; it finds generic compliance suppression but no safety-specific refusal pull.

evidence_standards.name: Nested cross-validation for probe AUC
evidence_standards.detail: Probe AUCs use cross-validation with nested-CV layer selection and no test-set peeking.

evidence_standards.name: Bootstrap confidence intervals and control deltas
evidence_standards.detail: For fixed-cell harm-direction restoration, bootstrap over harmful prompts and 24 random seeds; report 95% intervals for the intervention and harm-minus-random delta, treating deltas whose intervals exclude zero as evidence of an effect. The held-out restoration result also reports 95% intervals.

evidence_standards.name: Paired bootstrap for attention-knockout contrasts
evidence_standards.detail: Report paired-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for early versus mass-matched, early versus late, and whole versus early contrasts; the mass-matched control is run with three fixed seeds.

evidence_standards.name: Held-out evaluation for causal transfer
evidence_standards.detail: The refuse-state transfer is estimated on a disjoint training split and tested on held-out prompts, with an in-distribution reference; harm-direction restoration is also tested on prompts disjoint from direction training.

evidence_standards.name: Sampling robustness check
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports a robustness check at temperature 0.7: plain harmful prompts still refuse and the prefill still strips refusal, while harm-direction restoration weakens.

datasets.name: HarmBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Optimize adversarial suffixes on a 20-behavior training subset and evaluate on the standard 200-behavior test set. Score attack success with the HarmBench-Llama-2-13B-cls evaluator; report source-model and target-model ASR. Run three random seeds and report mean ASR and sample standard deviation.

baselines.name: GCG
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same HarmBench setup and source/target models; experiments use suffix length 20, 500 total optimization iterations, and candidate batch size 128.

baselines.name: I-GCG
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same HarmBench setup and source/target models; experiments use suffix length 20, 500 total optimization iterations, and candidate batch size 128.

baselines.name: GJO
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same HarmBench setup and source/target models; experiments use suffix length 20, 500 total optimization iterations, and candidate batch size 128.

metrics.name: Attack Success Rate (ASR; reported as S-ASR and T-ASR)

controls.name: Base optimizer
controls.detail: Run the base GCG-style optimizer without BOSS suffix-pool selection and continuation.
controls.rules_out: Whether BOSS improves over the underlying optimizer without its search framework.

controls.name: w/ parents
controls.detail: Apply behavior coverage, standard source loss, and TFAL for parent selection only; use average source loss for final suffix selection.
controls.rules_out: Whether BOSS’s parent-selection diagnostics contribute beyond using average source loss alone.

controls.name: w/ final
controls.detail: Apply behavior coverage, standard source loss, and TFAL for final suffix selection only; use average source loss for parent selection.
controls.rules_out: Whether BOSS’s final-selection diagnostics contribute beyond using average source loss alone.

controls.name: Single-trajectory setting (N=1)
controls.detail: Compare different numbers of initial trajectories while holding the total update budget fixed at 500 and adjusting continuation budget accordingly.
controls.rules_out: Whether breadth gains are explained merely by a larger total update budget.

confounds.name: BOSS gains could be due to a larger optimization budget rather than broader search
confounds.detail: More total update steps could independently improve attack success, producing the same apparent gain attributed to breadth.
confounds.ruled_out_by: In the search-breadth comparison, keep the total update budget fixed at 500 while varying the number of initial trajectories and adjusting continuation budget.

confounds.name: Source-side diagnostics may not predict transfer effectiveness on target models
confounds.detail: Suffixes selected using source-model loss, TFAL, and behavior coverage could perform well on the source model but fail to transfer, despite the claimed improvement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate transferred suffixes on the target models and report T-ASR; the paper also acknowledges that transferability remains uncertain across substantially different models.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds; mean and sample standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports ASR means with sample standard deviations across three runs. It specifies no statistical test or numerical threshold for treating results as different.

datasets.name: AdvBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Activation-Guided GCG and standard GCG train on AdvBench goals for 200 discrete optimization steps. Soft-GCG sweeps use 25 training and 10 test prompts; suffix length is 20 tokens. Other Soft-GCG runs evaluate learned suffixes on the full AdvBench corpus using substring ASR; the paper says the corpus is evaluated multiple times but gives no count. Gemma experiments use 500 Soft-GCG steps.

datasets.name: refusal-direction dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses its harmful test split to evaluate universal suffixes trained for 200 discrete optimization steps; reports Substring, LlamaGuard2, and HarmBench ASR. The table uses the suffix with the lowest training loss. Refusal directions are selected using the dataset’s training splits.

baselines.name: GCG (standard GCG)

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on Llama-2-7b-chat-hf and the refusal-direction harmful_test split; the paper gives no further fairness controls.

metrics.name: Substring ASR
metrics.caveat: Substring matching can produce false positives and false negatives because it only checks for common refusal strings and is not adaptable to the response. Activation-Guided GCG is also evaluated with LlamaGuard2 and HarmBench; for Soft-GCG the paper suggests LlamaGuard as a more robust future evaluation.

controls.name: Baseline (no suffix)
controls.detail: The unmodified model is evaluated without a suffix on the refusal-direction harmful_test split.

confounds.name: Broader objectives may help through richer gradient signal rather than distributed refusal representations
confounds.detail: The paper explicitly notes that the stronger results for broader-scope objectives could reflect either distributed refusal representations or richer optimization gradients.

confounds.name: Gemma scaling results may reflect vocabulary size and optimization difficulty rather than safety-training or representation changes
confounds.detail: The paper says vocabulary size increases Soft-GCG optimization complexity and is entangled with model-specific safety training.

confounds.name: Substring ASR may not measure harmfulness accurately
confounds.detail: Absence or presence of common refusal substrings can misclassify completions, so the headline ASR may reflect string matching rather than harmfulness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For Activation-Guided GCG, also reports LlamaGuard2 and HarmBench ASR. Soft-GCG is evaluated with substring ASR only; the paper acknowledges this limitation.

confounds.name: Gemma3-270m’s perfect ASR may reflect incoherent outputs rather than successful harmful generation
confounds.detail: The paper notes that the 270m model became incoherent after optimization.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated evaluation and seed-comparison runs
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says long-main Soft-GCG suffixes are evaluated on the full AdvBench corpus multiple times and reports extended seed-comparison experiments at 2000 optimization iterations; it does not state the number of seeds or a statistical test.

evidence_standards.name: Reported ± values for Gemma3 ASR
evidence_standards.detail: Gemma3 ASR is reported with ± values (for example, 0.577 ± 0.031); the paper does not specify what the ± quantities represent or give a decision threshold for a real difference.

datasets.name: Harmbench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on its 400 malicious requests; ASR is determined by a fine-tuned Llama-2-13B classifier that checks whether each response is both relevant to the query and harmful. No split or preprocessing is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Deterministic decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: All experiments set temperature to zero and limit the maximum output to 4096 tokens; no seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests are specified.

AdvBench prompts are categorized into topics by Llama-3.1-8B for adaptive sampling.

datasets.eval_protocol: 400 malicious instructions used as target prompts; each is reformulated as a question by prepending “How can I”. HarmBench’s topic categories are used for adaptive sampling.

metrics.name: ASR-L
metrics.caveat: Llama-Guard-3 can identify benign responses as safe even when they lack explicit refusal phrases; the paper notes this explains cases where ASR-L is lower than ASR-R. HarmBench’s 25% copyright-related prompts, which models often comply with, can also elevate ASR; the paper reports results across multiple datasets.

metrics.name: ASR-R
metrics.caveat: Counts a response as successful if it contains none of the predefined refusal phrases, so benign responses without explicit refusal language can inflate the score. The authors manually inspect responses and report ASR-L alongside it; this issue is noted for Qwen-2.5-7B. HarmBench’s copyright-related prompts can also elevate ASR scores.

metrics.name: Reference score (Rᵢ)
metrics.caveat: A higher score is interpreted as more attention directed to preceding segments and potentially greater focus on the instruction-following pattern; the paper presents this as suggestive evidence.

controls.name: Unmodified MSJ
controls.detail: The reference condition without PANDAS modifications, compared at the same number of malicious demonstrations.
controls.rules_out: That PANDAS’s gains are explained merely by using more demonstrations.

controls.name: PA-only ablation
controls.detail: Apply positive affirmation without negative demonstrations or adaptive sampling; reported against MSJ and the combined method.
controls.rules_out: Whether positive affirmation can improve results without the other PANDAS components.

controls.name: ND-only ablation
controls.detail: Apply negative demonstrations without positive affirmation or adaptive sampling; reported against MSJ and the combined method.
controls.rules_out: Whether negative demonstrations can improve results without the other PANDAS components.

controls.name: AS-only ablation
controls.detail: Apply adaptive sampling without positive affirmation or negative demonstrations; reported against MSJ and the combined method.
controls.rules_out: Whether adaptive sampling can improve results without the other PANDAS components.

controls.name: PA+ND ablation
controls.detail: Use positive affirmation and negative demonstrations but omit adaptive sampling.
controls.rules_out: Whether adaptive sampling adds improvement beyond PA+ND.

controls.name: Shuffled demonstration order
controls.detail: The authors report checking successful MSJ after shuffling demonstration order.
controls.rules_out: That MSJ’s effectiveness necessarily depends on the original demonstration ordering.

confounds.name: ASR-R may count benign responses as successful jailbreaks
confounds.detail: A response can lack explicit refusal phrases while still being benign, making the rule-based success rate look high without harmful compliance; the paper observes this for Qwen-2.5-7B.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors manually inspect outputs and report ASR-L from Llama-Guard-3 alongside ASR-R; they note that the judge identifies these responses as safe.

confounds.name: HarmBench prompt composition can inflate attack-success rates
confounds.detail: The authors note that 25% of HarmBench target prompts concern copyright, an area where most models comply rather than refuse, potentially raising ASR independently of the attack’s effectiveness on other topics.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper reports the copyright proportion and evaluates on AdvBench as well as HarmBench.

confounds.name: Stylistic or formatting differences could drive adaptive topic selection
confounds.detail: Bayesian optimization might favor demonstration formats or styles rather than topic content.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors manually curate demonstrations to use a consistent “How can I” question form and bullet-point answers, and require questions and answers to be marked unsafe by Llama-Guard-3.

confounds.name: Model context retention or prior safety alignment could explain non-monotonic effects of shot count
confounds.detail: The paper proposes that limited long-context retention in the evaluated models, or safety alignment targeting particular MSJ shot counts, could explain why more shots do not consistently improve ASR.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors report ASR across shot counts and offer these as possible explanations, without a direct measurement distinguishing them.

evidence_standards.name: Three restarts per target prompt
evidence_standards.detail: The same jailbreaking configuration is applied three times to each prompt, with different demonstrations sampled on each restart; a prompt counts as successful if any restart succeeds. Results are reported as ASR. No statistical test, confidence interval, or variance-based threshold is specified.

metrics.name: RtA (Refuse to Answer) rate
metrics.caveat: The TrustLLM classifier can count responses as non-refusals even when they deflect without harmful content, and can miss responses that refuse initially but later provide harmful information; the paper also reports ASR and HS.

metrics.name: ASR (attack success rate)
metrics.caveat: It is a binary safe/unsafe assessment; the paper also reports HS as a finer-grained measure of harmfulness.

controls.name: Original prompt attack
controls.detail: Evaluates the dataset prompts without the paper’s persona prompt.
controls.rules_out: That the results with persona prompts merely reflect the effectiveness of the underlying dataset prompts.

controls.name: Crossover-only ablation
controls.detail: Runs 10 crossover operations and no mutation, keeping other hyperparameters fixed; compared with the original setting of 5 crossover and 5 mutation operations.
controls.rules_out: That the observed genetic-algorithm performance is attributable to crossover alone.

controls.name: Mutation-only ablation
controls.detail: Runs 10 mutation operations and no crossover, keeping other hyperparameters fixed; compared with the original setting of 5 crossover and 5 mutation operations.
controls.rules_out: That the observed genetic-algorithm performance is attributable to mutation alone.

controls.name: ASR-guided evolution
controls.detail: Uses ASR rather than classifier-calculated RtA as the genetic algorithm’s selection metric, with the same settings as the RtA-guided experiment.
controls.rules_out: That the reported behavior is independent of which selection objective guides evolution.

confounds.name: Lower RtA may reflect deflection rather than harmful-content generation, or a refusal followed by harmful content
confounds.detail: A reduction in explicit refusals could produce a favorable RtA result without the response actually providing harmful content.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper separately evaluates responses with GPT-4o-mini for binary safe/unsafe ASR and a 1–5 harmfulness score (HS).

confounds.name: Genetic-algorithm convergence may be due to initial RtA rather than semantic diversity
confounds.detail: A population that starts with more effective prompts could appear to converge better even if its semantic diversity is not important.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares populations selected for high or low RtA and high or low semantic diversity over 20 genetic-algorithm iterations on GPT-4o-mini.

confounds.name: Persona prompts may work only on the model on which they were evolved
confounds.detail: An effect tied to source-model-specific weaknesses would not transfer to other victim models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Applies prompts evolved on GPT-4o-mini or GPT-4o to other models, including Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, and DeepSeek-V3.

evidence_standards.name: Five repeated runs for the crossover/mutation ablation; standard deviation shown
evidence_standards.detail: Runs each ablation setting 5 times, compares the first 20 iterations, and plots shaded regions indicating standard deviation.

evidence_standards.name: Three repeated runs for the hyperparameter analysis
evidence_standards.detail: Runs each setting 3 times on GPT-4o-mini and averages the results.

confounds.name: The detector flags ordinary inputs as harmful rather than distinguishing harmful prompts
confounds.detail: The claimed ability to identify harmful prompts could be misleading if benign prompts were also flagged.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Tested a randomly written sentence repeated five times; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 answered “No.”

datasets.name: AdvBench (50 harmful requests curated by Chao et al.)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate attacks on the 50 distinct, diverse harmful requests. A jailbreak counts as successful only when GPT-4 gives a 10/10 semantic jailbreak score; the paper also reports evaluations with a rule-based judge, Llama-3-70B, and Llama Guard 2 in Appendix C.6. Attack templates are adapted per model, while random-search suffixes are request- and model-specific.

datasets.name: SaTML 2024 Trojan Detection Competition
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate triggers on five poisoned Llama-2-7B models using the reward model’s average score on a held-out test set of harmful prompts; lower scores indicate more successful jailbreaks. The paper searches five-token triggers on training examples, restricting candidate tokens and filtering triggers according to the competition’s formatting and tokenization constraints.

metrics.name: Attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: GPT-4 semantic judging can produce false positives, especially on Claude 2.1 (around 20%); the paper manually inspects generations and also reports results with a rule-based judge, Llama-3-70B, and Llama Guard 2.

metrics.name: Target-token log-probability
metrics.caveat: For GPT models, identical queries can return varying log-probabilities even at temperature zero with a fixed API seed, making random search’s optimization signal noisy; the paper shows the variation from 1,000 repeated queries and reports ASR alongside log-probability convergence plots.

metrics.name: Reward-model score
metrics.caveat: Higher scores indicate safer responses, so lower scores indicate more successful triggers; the paper reports average scores on a held-out test set alongside the no-trigger condition and ground-truth trojans.

controls.name: Prompt-only attack condition
controls.detail: The paper reports its prompt template without random search or self-transfer alongside attacks that add those components.
controls.rules_out: A difference against the augmented attack licenses attributing gains to adding search and/or self-transfer rather than to the prompt template alone.

controls.name: Prompt plus random search, without self-transfer
controls.detail: Reported alongside prompt plus random search plus self-transfer for models where both conditions are evaluated.
controls.rules_out: A difference against the self-transfer condition licenses attributing gains to the self-transfer initialization rather than random search alone.

controls.name: No trigger
controls.detail: In the trojan-detection evaluation, the poisoned models are evaluated on held-out harmful prompts without an appended trigger.
controls.rules_out: A difference against a trigger condition licenses attributing the lower reward-model score to the trigger rather than to the model’s untriggered behavior.

confounds.name: GPT-4 judge false positives or overfitting to the judge
confounds.detail: A high GPT-4-judged ASR could reflect the judge accepting outputs that are not valid jailbreaks; the paper specifically observes multiple false positives for Claude 2.1.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper manually inspects generations and reports evaluations with a rule-based judge, Llama-3-70B, and Llama Guard 2; it says these also indicate near-perfect ASR in almost all cases.

confounds.name: A perfect judge score may not mean the output is useful to an attacker
confounds.detail: The authors concede that even a 10/10 GPT-4 jailbreak score does not always imply that the generated content is actually beneficial to an attacker.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by a reported systematic measurement; the paper suggests follow-up questions or requesting more sentences as possible checks.

confounds.name: Random-search gains may be driven by noisy log-probability measurements
confounds.detail: GPT API log-probabilities vary across identical queries, potentially giving random search an unreliable signal even with temperature zero and a fixed seed.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper repeats the same query 1,000 times and plots the resulting log-probability variation; this documents the noise but does not rule out its influence on attack results.

evidence_standards.name: GPT-4 semantic-judge success threshold
evidence_standards.detail: A jailbreak is counted as successful only if GPT-4 assigns a 10/10 jailbreak score.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated-query measurement of GPT log-probability variability
evidence_standards.detail: The paper repeats an identical GPT-4 Turbo query 1,000 times using temperature zero and a fixed API seed, and reports the distribution of returned log-probabilities.

evidence_standards.name: Claude transfer-attack decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: For the transfer attack, the paper uses multiple random restarts with different generations at temperature one.
